text:
Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes

The triage app gives you the order to do things in, and this section is about doing them in a way that takes pressure off the person.

Anything that could let someone hurt themselves in the next five minutes takes priority, so get the car keys out of reach and turn the stove off, and move them away from roads and balconies, or pools of water for that matter. Letting them move around is fine, and pacing can help, but keep them from taking more of any substance. If they want to go confront somebody, that can wait. And if they want to leave, have someone go with them. Put any weapons away and keep the person away from crowds and strangers. If they want to post their big revelation about the universe, or message an ex, take the phone.

A lot of what looks like a deep psychedelic crisis is a scared person in a room that's getting on their nerves, so look around the room next. Maybe the light's too bright or the music's horrible. Are five concerned people talking at once? Somebody might be touching them and they hate it, or they're stuck beside someone they're wary of. And check whether they're too hot or too cold, or desperate for the bathroom.

They're feeling overwhelmed, so dim the lights, and clear out the extra people around them.

Then remind them where they are and what's happening, since a trip can make them lose track of it:

You're in [place]. It's [date/time]. You took [substance, if known], and its effects will peak and then change. It's intense right now, and it'll pass. We can sort out the rest of your life tomorrow.

If the state came from a practice, like meditation or fasting, the person can say:

I'm in an intense state, so I'm stopping the practice now, and my only job is to stay safe.

A state from a practice has no drug wearing off on a schedule, so there's no telling how long it will last. Once they can eat safely, food and warmth help their body settle.

Then help them pick one safe thing to try with their body and one calm person to stay with them, which the next two sections are about. Protect their sleep too, especially if they're euphoric or grandiose, and leave what it all meant until they've slept.
section: Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes
reader: someone sitting with a person on a bad psychedelic trip, or tripping themselves, who needs to know what to do in the first five minutes: dangers first, then the room, then what to say

placement: the Psychological First Aid section of the Shadow Work part, before Stillness or Movement? and Get One Human Anchor, which its last paragraph points to

questions.Q1: PASS: each paragraph opens on its point: the section's job, the first priority, the room's role, the reason for the fixes, what the script is for, what a practice state does, what comes next
questions.Q2: PASS: every act is the helper's or the person's own, with its purpose
questions.Q3: PASS: which things exactly: keys, stove, roads, balconies, pools; the light and the crowd; a practice like meditation or fasting
questions.Q4: PASS: no terms a reader wouldn't know; the triage app is linked where it is named
questions.Q5: PASS: each so turns on what's said before it
questions.Q6: PASS: dangers, room, what to say, the practice case with its own care, then what comes next
questions.Q7: PASS: every fact is about the person in front of them now
questions.Q8: PASS: the practice case's script and care sit together; the pointer to the next sections closes the section
questions.Q9: PASS: nothing compressed: the scripts are short lines meant to be said, the rest one step a sentence

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone?
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
